title: Baricitinib in adults of African descent with central centrifugal cicatricial alopecia (CCCA): completed phase 2, results not yet posted
headline: A single-arm, open-label phase 2 study of oral baricitinib (a JAK inhibitor) in adults of African descent with biopsy-proven CCCA finished in April 2026 with 27 treated and 17 completing 52 weeks; no results or publication yet.
evidenceTier: Registry record read in full (ClinicalTrials.gov); no results posted, no publication found
fit: Relevant only to biopsy-confirmed scarring hair loss of this type. It is a prescription decision for a specialist; nothing here supports self-directed use.
displaces: Fits nowhere as a routine product. If a clinician ever considered it, it would be a specialist-led addition to, or replacement of, existing CCCA treatment.
estimateNote: Prices marked EST are my guesses, not looked up.
summaryPoints: Registry record (read in full): 52 weeks of baricitinib 4 mg daily, open-label, single arm; sponsor Raven Clinical Research with Eli Lilly as collaborator; started October 2024, completed April 2026. Primary outcome: change in an investigator global assessment of scalp hair loss at month 12.

All participants had to be of African descent with biopsy-proven CCCA; women only per the record. Exclusions follow the usual JAK-inhibitor screen: history of venous thromboembolism or high thrombosis risk, recent heart attack or stroke, active or latent infection, malignancy, kidney impairment.
No control arm, so any improvement cannot be separated from the natural course of a slow, scarring condition (my inference). Treat as a signal to watch for results, not as evidence of benefit.

Related items surfaced in PubMed this run, abstracts not available to me: a retrospective review of low-dose oral metformin in CCCA (response not predicted by insulin resistance) and a retrospective analysis of CCCA in children. Neither was read.
toneData: Enrolment required African descent; other tone data not applicable
fitLine: Race-specific condition and population; the evidence level is a registry entry only.
timeline: Study ran 52 weeks; results timeline unknown
